cards.q: Define the rhetorical situation.
cards.a: The set of circumstances surrounding any text: the writer, the audience, the purpose, the context, the message, and the exigence that prompted it. Every rhetorical choice answers to it.
cards.n: Q2 essays that ignore the situation drift into summary; every choice you analyze must be tied back to purpose and audience.
x: writer, audience, purpose, context, exigence, message

cards.q: Define exigence.
cards.a: The urgent problem, event, or condition that prompts a writer to speak or write now. It is the reason the text exists at all.
cards.n: Exigence is the trigger, not the topic. Ask: what happened that made silence impossible?
x: the reason the text was written

cards.q: Contrast exigence and occasion.
cards.a: Exigence is the underlying problem or urgency that demands a response; occasion is the specific event or setting in which the text is delivered. A funeral is the occasion; a nation's grief and division is the exigence.
cards.n: Students collapse these. The occasion is on the calendar; the exigence is in the world.

cards.q: Define occasion in the rhetorical situation.
cards.a: The specific time, place, and event at which a text is delivered or published, including the conventions that setting carries (a commencement, a eulogy, an op-ed after a verdict).
cards.n: Occasion sets genre expectations; a speaker who breaks them is making a rhetorical choice worth analyzing.

cards.q: Define audience in the rhetorical situation.
cards.a: The readers or listeners the writer intends to reach, defined by their values, beliefs, knowledge, and needs, not merely by who happens to be present.
cards.n: AP wants audience described by values and assumptions, not demographics alone.

cards.q: Contrast primary and secondary audience.
cards.a: The primary audience is the group the writer directly addresses and hopes to move; the secondary audience is anyone else who receives the text, such as the press, opponents, or posterity.
cards.n: Public speeches often argue past the room: the people present are primary, the nation reading tomorrow is secondary.

cards.q: Define purpose in the rhetorical situation.
cards.a: What the writer wants the text to accomplish with a specific audience: to persuade, warn, unify, commemorate, satirize, critique, or call to action.
cards.n: State purpose as an infinitive verb plus an audience effect; naming a purpose verb is the fastest route to a defensible thesis.

cards.q: Contrast purpose and message.
cards.a: Message is what the text says, its central claim or idea; purpose is what the writer wants that message to do to the audience. Message is content; purpose is intended effect.
cards.n: A thesis that only restates the message earns no credit for analysis; the purpose is what choices serve.

cards.q: Define message in the rhetorical situation.
cards.a: The central idea or claim a text communicates, the substance of what the writer is asserting about the subject.

cards.q: Define context in the rhetorical situation.
cards.a: The historical, cultural, political, and personal circumstances surrounding the text that shape how it is written and received, including what the audience already believes.
cards.n: Context is a lever, not decoration: it explains why a choice would land with THAT audience at THAT moment.

cards.q: Define writer (or speaker) as an element of the rhetorical situation.
cards.a: The person producing the text, along with the experiences, expertise, biases, and relationship to the audience that they bring to it and that shape their credibility.

cards.q: Contrast the author and the speaker of a text.
cards.a: The author is the real person who wrote the text; the speaker is the constructed voice inside it. An author may adopt a speaker whose views and tone differ sharply from their own, as in satire.
cards.n: Classic trap: reading Swift's narrator in A Modest Proposal as Swift himself. Always ask whose voice is speaking.

cards.q: Recall what each letter of SOAPSTone stands for.
cards.a: Speaker, Occasion, Audience, Purpose, Subject, Tone. It is a checklist for unpacking any text's rhetorical situation before analysis.
cards.n: Use it as a pre-writing scan on Q2, then discard it; SOAPSTone is a tool, not an essay structure.
x: Speaker Occasion Audience Purpose Subject Tone

cards.q: Define the rhetorical triangle.
cards.a: The model showing the three interlocking elements of any rhetorical act: the speaker (ethos), the audience (pathos), and the subject or message (logos). A change in one reshapes the others.
cards.n: The triangle maps appeals onto positions: ethos lives with the speaker, pathos with the audience, logos with the subject.

cards.q: Define ethos.
cards.a: The appeal to the credibility, authority, and character of the speaker. It persuades because the audience trusts the person making the claim.
cards.n: Ethos is granted by the audience, not asserted by the speaker; analyze how a text earns it.

cards.q: Explain four ways a writer establishes ethos.
cards.a: By citing relevant expertise or experience; by using accurate evidence and correct conventions; by acknowledging opposing views fairly; and by showing shared values or goodwill toward the audience.
cards.n: Conceding a point is an ethos move: fairness buys trust before the refutation lands.

cards.q: Name Aristotle's three components of ethos.
cards.a: Phronesis (practical wisdom or good sense), arete (virtue or good moral character), and eunoia (goodwill toward the audience).
cards.n: You will not be tested on the Greek, but the three angles give you precise language for how credibility is built.

cards.q: Define pathos.
cards.a: The appeal to the audience's emotions, values, and imagination, moving them to feel something that makes the writer's position compelling.
cards.n: Pathos is not weakness or manipulation by default; AP expects you to judge whether it fits purpose and audience.

cards.q: Explain four ways a writer establishes pathos.
cards.a: Through vivid imagery and sensory detail; through anecdote and narrative about individuals; through connotative, charged diction; and through appeals to shared values, fears, or hopes.
cards.n: Naming the device is not analysis. Say which emotion is produced and why that emotion serves the purpose.

cards.q: Define logos.
cards.a: The appeal to logic and reason: evidence, data, examples, definitions, and clear lines of reasoning that make a claim rationally persuasive.

cards.q: Explain four ways a writer establishes logos.
cards.a: By supplying statistics and data; by reasoning from cause to effect or example to generalization; by defining terms and drawing distinctions; and by structuring claims in a visible, orderly line of reasoning.
cards.n: Numbers alone are not logos; the reasoning that connects the number to the claim is.

cards.q: Define kairos.
cards.a: The appeal to timeliness: the sense that this argument is being made at exactly the right moment, seizing an opening the situation has created.
cards.n: Kairos is the bridge from exigence to persuasion; phrases like now is the time or we can wait no longer are kairos markers.

cards.q: Define appeal to authority.
cards.a: Support drawn from the testimony of an expert, institution, sacred text, or respected figure, borrowing that source's credibility for the writer's claim.
cards.n: It is legitimate when the authority is relevant and the audience already accepts it; it becomes a fallacy when neither holds.

cards.q: Identify the textual markers that signal a writer is building credibility.
cards.a: First-person experience with the subject, credentials named or implied, precise and correctly cited evidence, measured qualified language, fair summaries of opponents, and shared vocabulary or values with the audience.
cards.n: Spotting these markers converts a vague ethos claim into specific, scoreable commentary.

cards.q: Decide which appeal dominates when a speaker cites her thirty years as a nurse before arguing for staffing limits.
cards.a: Ethos. The credential establishes her authority and firsthand knowledge, making the audience willing to trust her claim before any data appears.
cards.n: Multiple appeals usually operate at once; identify the dominant one and explain what it does for the purpose.

cards.q: Define tone.
cards.a: The writer's or speaker's attitude toward the subject and audience, conveyed through diction, syntax, imagery, and detail (for example wry, indignant, reverent, clinical).
cards.n: Tone must be named with a precise adjective. Negative or positive is not a tone.

cards.q: Define mood.
cards.a: The emotional atmosphere a text creates in the reader, the feeling the writing evokes (somber, tense, hopeful).

cards.q: Contrast tone and mood.
cards.a: Tone is the writer's attitude toward the subject; mood is the emotional effect produced in the reader. A detached tone can create an unsettling mood.
cards.n: Memory hook: tone belongs to the speaker, mood belongs to you. They need not match, and the gap is often the point.

cards.q: Define voice in writing.
cards.a: The distinctive, recurring personality of a writer across a text or body of work, produced by habitual diction, syntax, rhythm, and stance.
cards.n: Tone shifts passage to passage; voice is the constant behind the shifts.

cards.q: Define persona.
cards.a: The constructed identity or role a writer adopts within a text, which may differ from the real author (the humble observer, the outraged citizen, the naive proposer).
cards.n: Persona is a rhetorical choice: ask why THIS mask serves THIS audience.

cards.q: Define register.
cards.a: The level of formality and the variety of language a writer selects for a situation, ranging from intimate and casual to consultative, formal, and ceremonial.
cards.n: A shift in register mid-text is a high-value observation; it usually signals a shift in intended relationship with the audience.

cards.q: Contrast formal and informal register and state what each does to writer-audience distance.
cards.a: Formal register uses elevated diction, complete constructions, and no slang, creating distance and authority. Informal register uses contractions, colloquialism, and short forms, closing distance and signaling solidarity.
cards.n: Distance is the analytic payoff: register controls how near the writer stands to the audience.

cards.q: Define diction.
cards.a: A writer's deliberate word choice, considered both individually and as a pattern, which shapes tone, ethos, and the audience's judgment of the subject.
cards.n: Analyze diction in clusters. One word is an example; a pattern of words is an argument.

cards.q: Define concrete diction and give an example.
cards.a: Words naming things perceivable by the senses, specific and physical. e.g. rusted chain-link fence, diesel, sleet.
cards.n: Effect: grounds an abstract claim in something the audience can see, which builds pathos and credibility at once.

cards.q: Define abstract diction and give an example.
cards.a: Words naming ideas, qualities, or conditions that cannot be perceived by the senses. e.g. justice, freedom, dignity, progress.
cards.n: Effect: elevates a specific dispute into a matter of shared principle, but risks vagueness if never grounded.

cards.q: Contrast concrete and abstract diction in terms of rhetorical effect.
cards.a: Concrete diction makes an argument vivid, verifiable, and emotionally immediate; abstract diction makes it broad, principled, and quotable. Skilled writers alternate: the image proves, the abstraction generalizes.
cards.n: Noticing the pivot from concrete to abstract is a reliable source of sophisticated commentary.

cards.q: Define denotation.
cards.a: The literal, dictionary meaning of a word, independent of emotional association.

cards.q: Define connotation and give an example.
cards.a: The emotional, cultural, and evaluative associations a word carries beyond its literal meaning. e.g. thrifty, frugal, and stingy all denote careful with money but connote praise, neutrality, and blame.
cards.n: Effect: connotation lets a writer render a verdict while appearing merely to describe.

cards.q: Contrast denotation and connotation.
cards.a: Denotation is what a word means; connotation is what a word suggests. Two words can share a denotation while carrying opposite connotations, as with undocumented immigrant and illegal alien.
cards.n: When a passage seems neutral, check connotation. That is usually where the argument is hiding.

cards.q: Define colloquial diction and give an example.
cards.a: Informal, conversational word choice drawn from everyday speech. e.g. kind of a mess, no big deal, y'all.
cards.n: Effect: closes the gap with the audience and signals sincerity or shared identity; can cost authority with a formal audience.

cards.q: Define vernacular.
cards.a: The everyday language of a particular region, group, or class, including its distinctive grammar and idiom, as opposed to standardized or literary language.
cards.n: Effect: writing in the vernacular asserts that a community's own speech is worthy of the page, which is itself an argument about status.

cards.q: Define jargon and give an example.
cards.a: Specialized vocabulary belonging to a profession or field. e.g. amortization, titrate, tort, subordinate clause.
cards.n: Effect: signals insider expertise to specialists but excludes general audiences; excluding can itself be the point.

cards.q: Define euphemism and give an example.
cards.a: A mild or indirect expression substituted for one considered harsh, blunt, or offensive. e.g. downsizing for firing; collateral damage for civilian deaths.
cards.n: Effect: softens or conceals; analyzing euphemism means asking what the softer word is protecting the audience from noticing.

cards.q: Define pedantic diction.
cards.a: Word choice that is ostentatiously scholarly, bookish, or overly precise, calling attention to the speaker's learning.
cards.n: Effect: can build authority with an academic audience or, when a persona is being mocked, expose the speaker as pompous.

cards.q: Define the rhetorical purpose to critique.
cards.a: To evaluate a subject by exposing its flaws or limits, usually with an implied standard the subject fails to meet. It judges rather than merely describes.
cards.n: Critique implies a standard. Name the standard and your commentary immediately deepens.

cards.q: Define the rhetorical purpose to satirize.
cards.a: To ridicule a person, institution, or practice through irony, exaggeration, or mockery in order to expose folly or vice and imply the need for reform.
cards.n: Satire always has a corrective target; if you cannot name what should change, you have not found the purpose.

cards.q: Define the rhetorical purpose to commemorate.
cards.a: To honor a person, group, or event publicly, affirming shared values and fixing the subject's meaning in collective memory.
cards.n: Commemorative texts are rarely only praise; eulogies and dedications usually convert memory into a call to act.

cards.q: Define the rhetorical purpose to warn.
cards.a: To alert an audience to a danger or likely consequence so that they change course before it arrives.
cards.n: Warning depends on kairos: the threat must feel near enough to matter and far enough to prevent.

cards.q: Define the rhetorical purpose to persuade.
cards.a: To move an audience to accept a claim, adopt an attitude, or take a specific action by giving them reasons and motives to do so.

cards.q: Define the rhetorical purpose to unify.
cards.a: To bind a divided or diverse audience into a single group by invoking shared values, common history, or a common threat.
cards.n: Watch for first-person plural: a shift to we is the grammatical machinery of unification.

cards.q: Apply the correct purpose verb: a senator recounts a factory closure, then urges passage of a retraining bill.
cards.a: The purpose is to persuade the audience to support the bill; the anecdote serves that purpose by making the abstract policy a human loss. A verb such as to move or to spur to action also fits.
cards.n: A strong Q2 thesis names the purpose verb and the audience effect, not the list of devices.

cards.q: Explain what is meant by audience assumptions.
cards.a: The beliefs, knowledge, and attitudes a writer takes for granted that the audience already holds, which the text builds on without arguing for them.
cards.n: Unstated assumptions are where arguments are strongest and most vulnerable; naming one is a sophistication move.

cards.q: Define shared values in rhetoric.
cards.a: Principles the writer and audience already hold in common, such as fairness, family, freedom, or sacrifice, which a writer invokes as agreed ground from which to argue.
cards.n: Appeals to shared values operate as both ethos and pathos: they prove the speaker is one of us and make the audience feel it.

cards.q: Define common ground in an argument.
cards.a: The area of agreement a writer establishes with a resistant audience before advancing a contested claim, so the disagreement looks narrower than it seemed.
cards.n: Common ground is a strategic concession: it buys a hearing.

cards.q: Apply audience analysis: what four questions should you ask before analyzing a speaker's choices?
cards.a: Who is the intended audience? What do they already believe about this subject? What do they value? What might make them resist? Each choice should then be explained as an answer to those conditions.
cards.n: This is the engine of Row B commentary: choice, audience condition, effect.

cards.q: Define bias as it applies to a source or speaker.
cards.a: A predisposition, interest, or perspective that shapes what a writer notices, includes, and omits. It is not automatically a flaw, but it conditions how evidence should be weighed.
cards.n: On the synthesis question, naming a source's stake is stronger than dismissing it as biased.

cards.q: Define counterargument.
cards.a: A position opposing the writer's claim, presented within the text so the writer can address it. It represents the strongest objection an informed opponent would raise.
cards.n: Introducing a counterargument builds ethos: it shows the writer has considered more than one side.

cards.q: Define concession.
cards.a: Granting that some part of an opposing view is true, reasonable, or well intentioned, before returning to and reasserting one's own position.
cards.n: Signal words: admittedly, granted, of course, it is true that. Concession almost always sets up a but.

cards.q: Define refutation.
cards.a: Directly disproving or discrediting an opposing argument by attacking its evidence, its reasoning, or its assumptions.

cards.q: Define rebuttal.
cards.a: The writer's response to an anticipated objection, explaining why the objection does not defeat the claim. It typically follows a concession and may include refutation.
cards.n: Rebuttal is the answer; refutation is the demolition. A rebuttal can concede a point and still stand.

cards.q: Contrast concession and refutation.
cards.a: A concession grants that an opposing point has merit; a refutation argues that the opposing point is wrong. Used together, concession earns trust and refutation reclaims the ground.
cards.n: The concession-refutation pair is the most common structural move on Q3; label it and explain what the sequence does to a skeptical reader.

cards.q: Contrast counterargument and rebuttal.
cards.a: The counterargument is the opposing position itself, stated by the writer; the rebuttal is the writer's reply to it. One raises the objection, the other answers it.

cards.q: Define qualification of a claim.
cards.a: Limiting the scope, certainty, or conditions of a claim so it can withstand objection, using words such as often, in most cases, unless, or largely.
cards.n: A qualified claim is stronger, not weaker: it is harder to disprove and signals intellectual honesty.

cards.q: Identify eight qualifiers a writer can use to limit a claim.
cards.a: Often, usually, in most cases, tends to, may, largely, unless, with few exceptions. Each narrows the claim to what the evidence can actually support.
cards.n: On Q3, adding one qualifier to an absolute claim often rescues an overreaching thesis.

cards.q: Explain why a writer anticipates objections.
cards.a: Anticipating objections shows the writer understands the opposing view, defuses resistance before it hardens, and demonstrates fairness, which strengthens ethos and makes the audience more receptive to the claim.

cards.q: Define rhetorical choice.
cards.a: Any deliberate decision a writer makes (a word, a structure, an appeal, an omission) understood as selected in order to affect a specific audience for a specific purpose.
cards.n: Say chooses, not uses. The verb choose forces you to explain why, which is where the points are.

cards.q: Contrast identifying a strategy and explaining its effect.
cards.a: Identifying names the device (the speaker uses anaphora); explaining effect states what the choice does to the audience and how it advances the purpose (the repetition builds momentum that makes inaction feel indefensible).
cards.n: The AP rubric rewards effect, not labels. A device list with no effect stalls at the low end of Row B.

cards.q: Explain what a line of reasoning is in a rhetorical analysis essay.
cards.a: The sequence of claims about the writer's choices that, taken in order, supports the thesis. Each paragraph advances the argument about purpose rather than walking through the passage device by device.
cards.n: Chronological device-hunting is the most common Q2 failure; organize by the argument, not by the passage.

cards.q: Contrast commentary and summary in a rhetorical analysis.
cards.a: Summary restates what the text says; commentary explains why the writer made a choice and what it accomplishes with the audience. Only commentary earns Row B credit.
cards.n: Test: if a reader who never saw the passage learns only its content from your sentence, it is summary.

cards.q: State what makes a thesis defensible on the rhetorical analysis question.
cards.a: It must make an arguable claim about the writer's rhetorical choices and their relationship to purpose or message, rather than restating the prompt, listing devices, or summarizing the passage.
cards.n: Row A is one point and takes one sentence: name the purpose and the kind of choices that serve it.

cards.q: Recall what each row of the AP Lang FRQ rubric awards.
cards.a: Row A: thesis, 1 point. Row B: evidence and commentary, 4 points. Row C: sophistication, 1 point. Six points total per essay.
cards.n: Row B is where essays are won or lost; four of the six points ride on specific evidence plus explanation.

cards.q: Explain what earns the sophistication point.
cards.a: A consistently vivid and persuasive style, or genuine engagement with complexity: situating the argument in a broader context, exploring tensions and implications, or explaining the significance of a rhetorical situation. It cannot be earned by a phrase.
cards.n: Sophistication is a whole-essay quality; tacking on a broader implications sentence at the end rarely earns it.

cards.q: Apply the rhetorical situation to a photograph or political cartoon.
cards.a: Identify the image maker, the intended viewer, the exigence prompting publication, and the purpose; then treat framing, caption, symbols, exaggeration, and juxtaposition as the visual equivalents of rhetorical choices.
cards.n: Synthesis sources include visuals; they must be analyzed and cited as arguments, not used as decoration.

cards.q: Define style in rhetorical analysis.
cards.a: The characteristic way a writer uses language: the combined effect of diction, syntax, imagery, figurative language, and tone that distinguishes one writer's prose from another's.
cards.n: Style is never neutral; every stylistic pattern is evidence of an attitude toward the subject and audience.

cards.q: Define syntax.
cards.a: The arrangement of words, phrases, and clauses within sentences, including sentence length, type, and order of elements.
cards.n: Syntax commentary is the fastest way out of a diction-only essay; describe the pattern, then its effect.

cards.q: Identify what a shift (or pivot) in a passage is and how to spot one.
cards.a: A point where tone, diction, syntax, or perspective changes direction. Markers include but, yet, however, a paragraph break, a change in verb tense or person, or a sudden short sentence after long ones.
cards.n: Shifts are gold on Q2: analyze what changes and why the writer needed the audience moved at that moment.

cards.q: Define anaphora and give an example.
cards.a: Repetition of the same word or phrase at the beginning of successive clauses or sentences. e.g. We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds, we shall fight in the fields.
cards.n: Effect: builds rhythm and cumulative momentum, drilling the repeated idea into memory and making the claim feel inevitable.

cards.q: Define epistrophe and give an example.
cards.a: Repetition of the same word or phrase at the end of successive clauses. e.g. government of the people, by the people, for the people.
cards.n: Effect: lands the emphasis on the repeated term, so the audience leaves holding that word rather than the ones around it.

cards.q: Define symploce and give an example.
cards.a: Anaphora and epistrophe combined: successive clauses begin with the same word and end with the same word. e.g. When there is talk of hatred, let us stand against it; when there is talk of violence, let us stand against it.
cards.n: Effect: the fixed frame spotlights the one element that changes, making the varied middle term feel like the true subject.

cards.q: Define anadiplosis and give an example.
cards.a: Repetition of the last word of one clause at the beginning of the next. e.g. Fear leads to anger; anger leads to hate; hate leads to suffering.
cards.n: Effect: chains the ideas into a causal sequence, so a contestable claim feels like logical dominoes falling.

cards.q: Define epanalepsis and give an example.
cards.a: Repetition of the same word or phrase at both the beginning and the end of a clause or sentence. e.g. Nothing is worse than doing nothing.
cards.n: Effect: closes the sentence in a circle, creating a sense of inescapability or of returning to an unavoidable fact.

cards.q: Define epizeuxis and give an example.
cards.a: Immediate repetition of a word with no words in between. e.g. Never, never, never give up.
cards.n: Effect: raw intensification that reads as emotion rather than argument, conveying urgency the sentence's content alone would not.

cards.q: Define repetition as a rhetorical strategy and give an example.
cards.a: Deliberate reuse of a word, phrase, or structure for emphasis rather than by accident. e.g. Free at last, free at last, thank God Almighty, we are free at last.
cards.n: Effect: marks what matters, creates rhythm the ear remembers, and unifies a passage around a single idea.

cards.q: Define antithesis and give an example.
cards.a: Contrasting ideas set against each other in parallel grammatical structure. e.g. That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.
cards.n: Effect: sharpens a messy issue into two clean opposites and makes the speaker sound balanced and decisive.

cards.q: Define chiasmus and give an example.
cards.a: A reversal of grammatical structure in two successive phrases, in an ABBA pattern, without necessarily repeating the same words. e.g. By day the frolic, and the dance by night.
cards.n: Effect: the mirrored shape feels designed and inevitable, lending an ordinary observation the weight of a maxim.

cards.q: Define antimetabole and give an example.
cards.a: Repetition of the same words in reverse grammatical order. e.g. Ask not what your country can do for you; ask what you can do for your country.
cards.n: Effect: the reversal makes the idea feel discovered rather than asserted, and its symmetry makes it endlessly quotable.

cards.q: Contrast chiasmus and antimetabole.
cards.a: Both invert structure in an ABBA pattern, but antimetabole repeats the identical words in reverse order, while chiasmus reverses only the grammatical structure. Every antimetabole is a chiasmus; not every chiasmus is an antimetabole.
cards.n: If the same words come back flipped, name it antimetabole; if only the shape flips, chiasmus is safer.

cards.q: Define parallelism and give an example.
cards.a: Using the same grammatical form for elements of equal importance. e.g. reading widely, writing daily, and thinking carefully.
cards.n: Effect: signals that the items carry equal weight and makes complex material easy to follow, which reads as control and authority.

cards.q: Define isocolon and give an example.
cards.a: Parallel elements that are also equal in length and rhythm. e.g. Buy it, use it, break it, fix it.
cards.n: Effect: the metrical evenness makes a line sound engineered and sloganlike, easy to chant and hard to forget.

cards.q: Define tricolon and give an example.
cards.a: A series of three parallel words, phrases, or clauses. e.g. life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.
cards.n: Effect: three feels complete to the ear; when the third element is longest (ascending tricolon), the series builds to a climax.

cards.q: Define zeugma and give an example.
cards.a: A construction in which one word, usually a verb, governs two or more others, often in different senses. e.g. She stole his wallet and his heart.
cards.n: Effect: compresses the literal and figurative into one stroke, producing wit or an ironic equation of unlike things.

cards.q: Define asyndeton and give an example.
cards.a: Deliberate omission of conjunctions between coordinated words, phrases, or clauses. e.g. I came, I saw, I conquered.
cards.n: Effect: accelerates the pace and makes a list feel breathless or open-ended, as if it could continue indefinitely.

cards.q: Define polysyndeton and give an example.
cards.a: Deliberate repetition of conjunctions between every item in a series. e.g. and the rain and the wind and the cold and the dark.
cards.n: Effect: slows the pace and piles items up so the accumulation feels overwhelming, exhausting, or relentless.

cards.q: Contrast the effects of asyndeton and polysyndeton.
cards.a: Asyndeton removes conjunctions to speed the sentence and suggest an incomplete, urgent list; polysyndeton adds conjunctions to slow the sentence and make the list feel heavy and unending. Both alter pace, in opposite directions.
cards.n: Both are about pacing; if you can say faster or slower and why that matters here, you have real commentary.

cards.q: Define ellipsis as a syntactic device and give an example.
cards.a: Omission of words the reader can supply from context. e.g. Some students go to the library; others, to the gym.
cards.n: Effect: tightens and quickens the prose and flatters readers by trusting them to fill the gap.

cards.q: Define metaphor and give an example.
cards.a: A direct comparison asserting that one thing is another, without like or as. e.g. Time is a thief.
cards.n: Effect: transfers the connotations of the comparison onto the subject, quietly framing how the audience should judge it.

cards.q: Define simile and give an example.
cards.a: A comparison of two unlike things using like or as. e.g. The room went as quiet as a chapel.
cards.n: Effect: makes the unfamiliar concrete while keeping the comparison explicit and limited, so the writer controls how far it extends.

cards.q: Define analogy and give an example.
cards.a: An extended comparison that maps the relationship in a familiar case onto an unfamiliar one in order to explain or argue. e.g. Running a national budget is like running a household budget.
cards.n: Effect: makes complex reasoning accessible, but it is only as strong as the mapping; a broken mapping is a false analogy.

cards.q: Define extended metaphor and give an example.
cards.a: A single metaphor sustained across several sentences or an entire passage, with its details developed. e.g. describing a political campaign as a voyage, then continuing with charts, storms, mutiny, and landfall.
cards.n: Effect: supplies a controlling frame the reader keeps interpreting through, so the comparison shapes an entire argument, not one line.

cards.q: Define conceit and give an example.
cards.a: An elaborate, surprising extended metaphor linking two strikingly unlike things. e.g. Donne comparing two lovers to the twin legs of a drawing compass.
cards.n: Effect: displays ingenuity and forces the reader to grant an unexpected likeness, making the writer's cleverness part of the appeal.

cards.q: Define metonymy and give an example.
cards.a: Substituting the name of something closely associated with a thing for the thing itself. e.g. The White House announced new sanctions; the crown demanded taxes.
cards.n: Effect: compresses an institution into a single image and can deflect responsibility from the actual people acting.

cards.q: Define synecdoche and give an example.
cards.a: A figure in which a part stands for the whole or a whole stands for a part. e.g. All hands on deck; boots on the ground.
cards.n: Effect: focuses attention on the relevant part, which can heroize (hands as labor) or dehumanize (boots as soldiers).

cards.q: Contrast metonymy and synecdoche.
cards.a: Synecdoche substitutes a part of the thing for the whole (hands for sailors); metonymy substitutes something associated with but not part of the thing (the crown for the monarchy). Synecdoche is a subset of substitution by part.
cards.n: If the substituted word names a physical piece of the thing, call it synecdoche; if it is merely linked to it, metonymy.

cards.q: Define hyperbole and give an example.
cards.a: Deliberate exaggeration for effect, not intended to be taken literally. e.g. I have explained this a million times.
cards.n: Effect: signals the intensity of the speaker's feeling and can generate humor or expose an opponent's position as absurd.

cards.q: Define understatement and give an example.
cards.a: Presenting something as smaller or less significant than it actually is. e.g. calling a category five hurricane a bit of weather.
cards.n: Effect: the gap between event and description does the work, conveying composure, dark humor, or contempt.

cards.q: Define litotes and give an example.
cards.a: A form of understatement that affirms something by negating its opposite. e.g. She is no fool; the results were not bad.
cards.n: Effect: makes praise or criticism sound measured and restrained, which reads as confidence rather than enthusiasm.

cards.q: Define verbal irony and give an example.
cards.a: Saying the opposite of what is meant, with the gap available to the audience. e.g. remarking What lovely weather during a downpour.
cards.n: Effect: creates complicity with the audience who catch the gap, forming an in-group that shares the speaker's judgment.

cards.q: Define situational irony and give an example.
cards.a: A discrepancy between what is expected to happen and what actually happens. e.g. a fire station burning down.
cards.n: Effect: exposes the distance between human plans and outcomes, which writers use to critique confidence or systems.

cards.q: Define dramatic irony and give an example.
cards.a: A situation in which the audience knows something a character does not. e.g. Oedipus vowing to punish the murderer the audience knows is himself.
cards.n: Effect: builds tension and places the audience in a superior position, inviting judgment of the unknowing figure.

cards.q: Define sarcasm and give an example.
cards.a: Sharp, mocking verbal irony aimed at a target, usually marked by tone of voice. e.g. saying Nice work after someone drops the tray.
cards.n: Effect: wounds or belittles the target and can alienate audiences who identify with it, unlike gentler verbal irony.

cards.q: Define satire and give an example.
cards.a: A mode that uses irony, exaggeration, or ridicule to expose vice, folly, or abuse, implying that reform is needed. e.g. Swift's A Modest Proposal.
cards.n: Effect: turns laughter into leverage, shaming an audience toward change while letting the writer avoid direct accusation.

cards.q: Define Horatian satire and give an example.
cards.a: Gentle, playful, amused satire that laughs with human folly rather than condemning it. e.g. a light send-up of parents obsessed with youth sports.
cards.n: Effect: keeps the audience comfortable enough to recognize themselves in the target instead of getting defensive.

cards.q: Define Juvenalian satire and give an example.
cards.a: Bitter, indignant, moralizing satire that treats its target with contempt. e.g. Swift's proposal that the poor sell their children as food.
cards.n: Effect: provokes outrage rather than laughter, positioning the target as a moral offense demanding response.

cards.q: Contrast Horatian and Juvenalian satire.
cards.a: Horatian satire is light, witty, and tolerant, treating folly as laughable and human; Juvenalian satire is harsh, bitter, and moralizing, treating vice as intolerable. The difference is tone and the severity of the implied indictment.
cards.n: Naming which kind of satire, and why the writer needed that severity for that audience, is a strong sophistication move.

cards.q: Define paradox and give an example.
cards.a: A statement that appears self-contradictory yet reveals a truth on reflection. e.g. The more you learn, the more you realize how little you know.
cards.n: Effect: stalls the reader into rethinking, so the insight feels earned rather than handed over.

cards.q: Define oxymoron and give an example.
cards.a: Two contradictory terms placed side by side in a single phrase. e.g. deafening silence, bittersweet, cruel kindness.
cards.n: Effect: compresses tension into two words, signaling that the subject resists a simple label.

cards.q: Contrast paradox and oxymoron.
cards.a: An oxymoron is a compressed contradiction within a phrase (jumbo shrimp); a paradox is a full statement or situation that seems contradictory but proves meaningful. Scale is the difference: phrase versus proposition.
cards.n: Students label every paradox an oxymoron. If it is a whole idea rather than a two-word pair, call it paradox.

cards.q: Define allusion and give an example.
cards.a: A brief, indirect reference to a well-known person, text, event, or work, left unexplained. e.g. calling a costly victory his Waterloo.
cards.n: Effect: borrows the authority and emotion of a shared reference and quietly tests whether the audience belongs to that shared culture.

cards.q: Define apostrophe as a rhetorical device and give an example.
cards.a: Direct address to an absent person, an abstraction, or an inanimate thing. e.g. O Death, where is thy sting?
cards.n: Effect: raises the emotional pitch and dramatizes the speaker's relationship to the idea, making the audience witnesses to it.

cards.q: Define personification and give an example.
cards.a: Attributing human qualities or actions to an animal, object, or abstraction. e.g. The wind whispered through the pines; justice demands an answer.
cards.n: Effect: makes abstractions feel like agents with intentions, so the audience responds to an idea as it would to a person.

cards.q: Define imagery and give an example.
cards.a: Language that appeals to the senses (sight, sound, touch, taste, smell) to create a vivid experience. e.g. the sharp tang of diesel over wet asphalt.
cards.n: Effect: makes the audience experience a claim rather than merely accept it, which produces pathos without explicit emotional appeal.

cards.q: Define symbolism and give an example.
cards.a: The use of a concrete object, action, or image to represent an abstract idea. e.g. a flag standing for national identity and sacrifice.
cards.n: Effect: lets a writer argue about an abstraction through something the audience can see, feel, and already values.

cards.q: Define juxtaposition and give an example.
cards.a: Placing two contrasting elements side by side so the comparison is unavoidable. e.g. describing a gleaming new stadium and then the shuttered school across the street.
cards.n: Effect: the reader draws the comparison unaided, so the judgment feels self-generated rather than imposed by the writer.

cards.q: Define rhetorical question and give an example.
cards.a: A question asked for effect rather than to obtain an answer, because the answer is assumed. e.g. Are we to stand by and do nothing?
cards.n: Effect: recruits the audience into supplying the answer, so agreement feels like their own conclusion.

cards.q: Define hypophora and give an example.
cards.a: A device in which the writer raises a question and then immediately answers it. e.g. What must we do now? We must vote, and we must not stop there.
cards.n: Effect: seizes control of the agenda by anticipating the audience's question and casting the speaker as the one with answers.

cards.q: Define aporia and give an example.
cards.a: An expression of real or feigned doubt or uncertainty about how to proceed. e.g. I scarcely know where to begin, or what words could possibly be adequate.
cards.n: Effect: signals humility and sincerity, disarming a skeptical audience before the speaker makes a confident claim.

cards.q: Define alliteration and give an example.
cards.a: Repetition of initial consonant sounds in nearby words. e.g. a wild and windy winter west.
cards.n: Effect: binds words into a unit the ear treats as one idea, making the phrase memorable and quotable.

cards.q: Define assonance and give an example.
cards.a: Repetition of vowel sounds in nearby words. e.g. the light of the fire is a sight.
cards.n: Effect: creates internal music that slows the line and knits its words together without the emphasis of rhyme.

cards.q: Define consonance and give an example.
cards.a: Repetition of consonant sounds within or at the end of nearby words. e.g. the lumpy, bumpy road; pitter patter.
cards.n: Effect: adds subtle cohesion and can make a passage feel harsh or soft depending on which consonants recur.

cards.q: Define onomatopoeia and give an example.
cards.a: A word that imitates the sound it names. e.g. buzz, clang, hiss, thud.
cards.n: Effect: collapses distance by putting the reader inside the scene, hearing rather than being told.

cards.q: Define cacophony and give an example.
cards.a: A deliberately harsh, discordant arrangement of sounds. e.g. the cracked jackhammer clattered and scraped.
cards.n: Effect: makes the subject feel unpleasant or violent, so the sound of the prose delivers a verdict the words never state.

cards.q: Define euphony and give an example.
cards.a: A pleasing, harmonious arrangement of sounds, typically using soft consonants and long vowels. e.g. the low lull of the summer meadow.
cards.n: Effect: makes the subject feel calm or beautiful, aligning the reader's ear with the writer's approval.

cards.q: Define periodic sentence and give an example.
cards.a: A sentence in which the main clause is withheld until the end, after introductory modifiers. e.g. Despite the rain, the delays, and the cold that cut through every coat, we marched.
cards.n: Effect: creates suspense by making the reader hold the modifiers until the payoff, which lands the main idea with force.

cards.q: Define loose (cumulative) sentence and give an example.
cards.a: A sentence that states its main clause first and then adds modifying phrases. e.g. We marched, soaked to the skin, exhausted, still singing.
cards.n: Effect: feels natural and conversational, giving immediate clarity and then enriching it detail by detail.

cards.q: Contrast periodic and loose sentences by effect.
cards.a: The periodic sentence delays the main clause to build suspense and emphasize the ending; the loose or cumulative sentence delivers the main clause first and accumulates detail after, sounding relaxed and immediate.
cards.n: Naming which one a writer chose, and what the delay or the immediacy does to a reader, is textbook Row B commentary.

cards.q: Define balanced sentence and give an example.
cards.a: A sentence whose two halves are equal in grammatical structure and length, usually joined by a semicolon or conjunction. e.g. To err is human; to forgive, divine.
cards.n: Effect: equality of form implies equality of the ideas, giving the statement an authoritative, proverbial ring.

cards.q: Define simple sentence and give an example.
cards.a: A sentence containing one independent clause and no dependent clause. e.g. The bill failed.
cards.n: Effect: after a run of long sentences, a short simple sentence lands like a verdict, which is why writers save them for the turn.

cards.q: Define compound sentence and give an example.
cards.a: A sentence with two or more independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction or a semicolon. e.g. The bill failed, but the movement grew.
cards.n: Effect: grants the two ideas equal grammatical weight, presenting them as parallel realities rather than ranking them.

cards.q: Define complex sentence and give an example.
cards.a: A sentence with one independent clause and at least one dependent clause. e.g. Although the bill failed, the movement grew.
cards.n: Effect: subordination ranks the ideas; whatever sits in the independent clause is what the writer wants the reader to carry away.

cards.q: Define compound-complex sentence and give an example.
cards.a: A sentence with two or more independent clauses and at least one dependent clause. e.g. Although the bill failed, the movement grew, and new donors appeared.
cards.n: Effect: holds layered causation in a single breath, useful when a writer wants complexity to feel manageable.

cards.q: Define independent clause and give an example.
cards.a: A group of words with a subject and a verb that expresses a complete thought and can stand alone as a sentence. e.g. the jury returned a verdict.
cards.n: Effect: what a writer places in independent clauses is what the sentence asserts; everything else is framing.

cards.q: Define dependent (subordinate) clause and give an example.
cards.a: A clause with a subject and verb that cannot stand alone because it begins with a subordinating conjunction or relative pronoun. e.g. although the jury deliberated for six days.
cards.n: Effect: material placed in dependent clauses is demoted to background, a quiet way to concede a point without conceding emphasis.

cards.q: Define appositive and give an example.
cards.a: A noun or noun phrase placed beside another noun to rename or identify it. e.g. Marie Curie, a two-time Nobel laureate, refused to patent her method.
cards.n: Effect: smuggles credentials or evidence into a sentence without a new claim, which is quiet, efficient ethos building.

cards.q: Define absolute phrase and give an example.
cards.a: A phrase consisting of a noun plus a participle (with modifiers) that modifies an entire sentence rather than one word. e.g. Her hands trembling, she signed the paper.
cards.n: Effect: layers a cinematic detail onto the main action without subordinating it, so image and event arrive together.

cards.q: Define participial phrase and give an example.
cards.a: A phrase beginning with a present or past participle that functions as an adjective. e.g. Shouting over the crowd, she finished her sentence.
cards.n: Effect: packs action into modifiers so sentences stay dense and forward-moving instead of stopping for a second clause.

cards.q: Define subordination and give an example.
cards.a: Placing one idea in a dependent clause so that it supports rather than competes with the main clause. e.g. Because the data were incomplete, the panel withheld judgment.
cards.n: Effect: creates a hierarchy of importance, telling the reader which idea is the point and which is merely a condition.

cards.q: Define coordination and give an example.
cards.a: Joining grammatically equal elements with a coordinating conjunction (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so). e.g. The panel withheld judgment, and the report was delayed.
cards.n: Effect: presents ideas as equals, which can suggest accumulation or refuse to rank causes the writer does not want ranked.

cards.q: Contrast subordination and coordination as rhetorical choices.
cards.a: Coordination gives ideas equal weight and lets them accumulate; subordination ranks them, pushing one into the background as cause, condition, or concession. The choice reveals what the writer treats as the main point.
cards.n: Look for although and while clauses: a writer often buries the opposing view there and keeps the main clause for the claim.

cards.q: Explain the rhetorical effect of sentence variety.
cards.a: Varying sentence length and structure prevents monotony and creates emphasis by contrast: a short sentence among long ones stops the reader, and a long accumulating sentence after short ones can feel like mounting evidence or exhaustion.
cards.n: Never say the writer uses varied syntax and stop. Point to the specific contrast and what it makes the reader feel at that moment.

cards.q: Define the rhetorical use of the colon and give an example.
cards.a: A colon follows an independent clause to introduce a list, explanation, appositive, or quotation. e.g. The problem was simple: nobody had read the bill.
cards.n: Effect: it makes a promise and then delivers, so whatever follows the colon receives the spotlight.

cards.q: Define the rhetorical use of the semicolon and give an example.
cards.a: A semicolon joins two closely related independent clauses without a conjunction, or separates items in a complex list. e.g. The vote failed; the coalition held anyway.
cards.n: Effect: asserts a tight logical relationship without naming it, forcing the reader to infer the connection.

cards.q: Define the rhetorical use of the dash and give an example.
cards.a: A dash sets off an interruption, an appositive, or an emphatic addition. e.g. The committee agreed on one thing — and only one — that time had run out.
cards.n: Effect: creates the feel of speech breaking in, giving the set-off material sudden emphasis or the intimacy of an aside.

cards.q: Define the rhetorical use of parentheses and give an example.
cards.a: Parentheses enclose supplementary material that is not part of the main structure. e.g. The measure passed (barely) on the third vote.
cards.n: Effect: lowers the volume, marking the material as an aside, a qualification, or a wry comment the writer will not elevate.

cards.q: Define anastrophe (syntactic inversion) and give an example.
cards.a: Reversal of normal word order for emphasis or effect. e.g. Powerful you have become; into the valley of death rode the six hundred.
cards.n: Effect: throws stress onto the fronted element and lends the voice an elevated, formal, or archaic quality.

cards.q: Define active voice and give an example.
cards.a: A construction in which the grammatical subject performs the action. e.g. The board rejected the proposal.
cards.n: Effect: assigns responsibility plainly and keeps prose direct, which reads as confidence and accountability.

cards.q: Define passive voice and give an example.
cards.a: A construction in which the subject receives the action; the actor appears in a by phrase or is omitted entirely. e.g. The proposal was rejected (by the board).
cards.n: Effect: shifts emphasis to the thing acted upon and can erase the actor, which is why bureaucratic prose favors it.

cards.q: Explain when passive voice is a deliberate rhetorical choice rather than a flaw.
cards.a: When the actor is unknown, obvious, or irrelevant; when the receiver of the action deserves emphasis; when the writer wants to maintain a neutral, institutional tone; or when the writer intends to obscure responsibility, as in mistakes were made.
cards.n: Do not call passive voice weak writing on the exam. Ask who disappears from the sentence and who benefits from that disappearance.

cards.q: Define polysemy and give an example.
cards.a: The capacity of a single word to carry multiple related meanings. e.g. right, meaning correct, a direction, and an entitlement.
cards.n: Effect: lets a writer play meanings against one another so a single word does double argumentative duty.

cards.q: Define pun and give an example.
cards.a: A play on words exploiting multiple meanings or similar sounds. e.g. A bicycle cannot stand on its own because it is two tired.
cards.n: Effect: humor lowers the audience's guard, and the display of wit builds the speaker's ethos as clever and quick.

cards.q: Define invective and give an example.
cards.a: Harsh, abusive denunciation of a person or thing, often in an extended verbal attack. e.g. Shakespeare's strings of insults such as you whoreson, beetle-headed knave.
cards.n: Effect: vents and incites indignation, rallying those who already agree while risking the appearance of unfairness to everyone else.

cards.q: Define colloquialism and give an example.
cards.a: An informal word or expression drawn from everyday speech, used in writing. e.g. gonna, no big deal, y'all.
cards.n: Effect: closes distance with the audience and signals authenticity or membership in a shared community.

cards.q: Define aphorism and give an example.
cards.a: A concise statement of a general truth or principle. e.g. A penny saved is a penny earned.
cards.n: Effect: sounds like inherited wisdom, so a contestable claim can slip past scrutiny as common sense.

cards.q: Define epigram and give an example.
cards.a: A brief, witty, often paradoxical saying. e.g. Wilde's I can resist everything except temptation.
cards.n: Effect: wit purchases credibility, and the memorable phrasing carries the argument further than the evidence alone would.

cards.q: Contrast aphorism and epigram.
cards.a: An aphorism states a general truth and aims at wisdom; an epigram aims at wit, usually with a paradoxical or surprising turn. Aphorisms instruct; epigrams delight, and often instruct by surprising.

cards.q: Define anecdote and give an example.
cards.a: A short account of a single incident, often personal, used to illustrate a point. e.g. opening an essay on health care with one patient's night in a waiting room.
cards.n: Effect: converts an abstract claim into a human case, producing pathos and the feel of evidence from a single instance.

cards.q: Define exemplum and give an example.
cards.a: A brief illustrative story or case cited to support a general claim or moral. e.g. citing Cincinnatus returning to his farm as proof that power can be surrendered.
cards.n: Effect: makes a general principle concrete and demonstrable, the classical form of arguing from example.

cards.q: Define a claim in argumentation.
cards.a: A claim is a debatable statement that the writer asks the audience to accept and then supports with evidence and reasoning. If no reasonable person could disagree with it, it is a fact, not a claim.
cards.n: The AP test for a claim is disagreement: if nobody could argue the other side, it cannot anchor an essay.

cards.q: Contrast a claim, a thesis, and an assertion.
cards.a: A claim is any debatable statement. A thesis is the single overarching claim that governs a whole text. An assertion is a statement offered without support - it becomes a claim only once evidence and reasoning back it.
cards.n: Readers penalize essays whose 'thesis' is really an unsupported assertion or a plain observation.

cards.q: Define a defensible thesis.
cards.a: A defensible thesis is a specific, arguable position that can be supported with available evidence. It takes a stance, previews a line of reasoning, and could be reasonably contested by an informed reader.
cards.n: Row A of every AP Lang rubric is won or lost here: defensible means arguable, not merely true.

cards.q: Identify what makes a thesis statement NOT defensible.
cards.a: It restates the prompt, states an obvious fact, merely announces a topic ('This essay will discuss...'), lists rhetorical devices with no message, or is so broad ('Since the dawn of time...') that no evidence could test it.
cards.n: Restating the prompt is the single most common Row A zero on the AP Lang exam.

cards.q: Define a claim of fact and give an example.
cards.a: A claim of fact argues that something is, was, or will be true, and is settled by evidence. Example: 'Standardized test scores have declined nationally since 2019.'

cards.q: Define a claim of value and give an example.
cards.a: A claim of value argues that something is good or bad, moral or immoral, better or worse, and depends on stated criteria. Example: 'Mandatory standardized testing is unfair to low-income students.'
cards.n: A value claim is only as strong as its criteria; strong writers name the standard they are judging by.

cards.q: Define a claim of policy and give an example.
cards.a: A claim of policy argues that a specific action should or should not be taken, and normally uses 'should' or 'must.' Example: 'States should stop requiring the SAT for public university admission.'
cards.n: Policy claims carry a hidden burden: you must show a problem exists AND that your solution is feasible.

cards.q: Decide the claim type: 'Social media harms adolescent mental health more than television ever did.'
cards.a: A claim of fact - it asserts a causal/comparative reality that evidence (studies, data) could confirm or disconfirm, rather than judging worth or urging action.

cards.q: Explain the role of a subclaim in an essay.
cards.a: A subclaim is a smaller arguable statement that supports the thesis; each body paragraph usually advances one. Together the subclaims form the line of reasoning that makes the thesis persuasive.

cards.q: Define evidence and state what it must do in an argument.
cards.a: Evidence is the specific material - data, examples, testimony, texts, experience - offered to support a claim. It must be relevant to the claim, sufficient in amount, and accurate, and it must be interpreted, not just dropped in.
cards.n: Relevant, sufficient, accurate: use these three words when a prompt asks you to assess evidence.

cards.q: Explain the strengths and limits of statistical evidence.
cards.a: Strength: statistics feel objective, scale up beyond one case, and persuade skeptical or data-minded audiences. Limits: they can be cherry-picked, decontextualized, or drawn from biased samples, and numbers alone do not establish causation.
cards.n: In MC questions, correlational data offered as proof of cause is a favorite wrong-reasoning trap.

cards.q: Explain the strengths and limits of anecdotal evidence.
cards.a: Strength: an anecdote is concrete, memorable, and emotionally engaging, so it humanizes abstract claims. Limit: one story is a sample of one and cannot establish a trend, which makes it vulnerable to the charge of hasty generalization.
cards.n: Anecdote plus data is the strong combination: the story makes the number matter.

cards.q: Explain the strengths and limits of expert testimony.
cards.a: Strength: borrowing a credentialed authority's ethos lends credibility on technical questions the audience cannot judge alone. Limit: it collapses if the expert is outside their field, biased, financially interested, or contradicted by other experts.
cards.n: Expert testimony is legitimate; appeal to authority is the fallacy version, where credentials replace reasons.

cards.q: Explain the strengths and limits of analogy as evidence.
cards.a: Strength: an analogy makes an unfamiliar idea intelligible by mapping it onto something the audience already accepts. Limit: it proves nothing on its own, and it fails if the two cases differ in the respect that actually matters.
cards.n: Analogy is an illustrative move, not a probative one; treat it as clarification plus a hypothesis.

cards.q: Explain the strengths and limits of historical example as evidence.
cards.a: Strength: a historical case shows that something has actually happened and supplies precedent and shared cultural weight. Limit: circumstances differ across eras, so the writer must argue that the past case is genuinely parallel.
cards.n: Strong AP argument essays use history but explicitly justify the comparison instead of assuming it.

cards.q: Explain the strengths and limits of personal experience as evidence.
cards.a: Strength: it grants firsthand authority and immediacy, especially on questions of lived effect. Limit: it is unverifiable, unrepresentative, and easy for an audience to dismiss as atypical.
cards.n: AP allows personal evidence on Q3, but it must be specific and analyzed - not a vague 'I have seen this happen.'

cards.q: Explain the strengths and limits of textual evidence.
cards.a: Strength: quoted or paraphrased text lets readers verify the claim against the source itself, which is essential in rhetorical analysis. Limit: quotations can be pulled out of context, over-quoted, or left unexplained.
cards.n: On Q2, textual evidence without commentary earns at most 1 of 4 in Row B.

cards.q: Decide which evidence type best persuades a skeptical policy audience and explain why.
cards.a: Data and expert testimony, because a skeptical policy audience wants verifiable scale and credentialed backing; anecdote is then added to make the numbers vivid rather than to carry the proof.
cards.n: Evidence selection is a rhetorical choice: the right evidence is the evidence that audience will accept.

cards.q: Contrast commentary and summary.
cards.a: Summary restates what the evidence says. Commentary explains what the evidence means, how it supports the claim, and why it matters. Commentary answers 'so what?'; summary answers only 'what?'
cards.n: The most common Row B ceiling on AP Lang essays is evidence plus summary instead of evidence plus commentary.

cards.q: Explain what a sentence of strong commentary must do.
cards.a: It must connect the specific evidence to the specific claim by naming the reasoning link - why this detail makes that claim more believable - and then tie back to the thesis or the writer's purpose.
cards.n: A reliable frame: 'This suggests... which supports... because...' Avoid 'This shows how important X is.'

cards.q: Define a warrant.
cards.a: A warrant is the underlying assumption, usually unstated, that licenses the move from evidence to claim - the principle that explains why this evidence counts as support for this claim.
cards.n: Test a warrant by asking: what would someone have to already believe for this evidence to prove this claim?

cards.q: Identify the warrant: 'The bridge is 70 years old, so it should be replaced.'
cards.a: The warrant is the unstated assumption that bridges of about 70 years old are unsafe or beyond their design life and that unsafe infrastructure ought to be replaced.

cards.q: Define backing in the Toulmin model.
cards.a: Backing is additional support offered for the warrant itself - evidence or reasoning that justifies the underlying assumption when the audience is unlikely to grant it automatically.

cards.q: Define a qualifier and give three examples.
cards.a: A qualifier limits the strength or scope of a claim, signaling how confident the writer is. Examples: 'usually,' 'in most urban districts,' 'likely.'
cards.n: Qualifiers make claims more defensible, not weaker: an unqualified absolute is easy to refute with one counterexample.

cards.q: Define the rebuttal (reservation) element of the Toulmin model.
cards.a: The rebuttal names the conditions under which the claim would not hold, or anticipates and answers the strongest objection to it.

cards.q: State the six elements of the Toulmin model.
cards.a: Claim, data (grounds/evidence), warrant, backing, qualifier, and rebuttal.
cards.n: Claim-data-warrant is the working core; backing, qualifier, and rebuttal are the refinements.
x: claim data warrant backing qualifier rebuttal

cards.q: Define Rogerian argument.
cards.a: Rogerian argument seeks common ground rather than victory: it states the opposing view fairly and sympathetically first, identifies shared values and the contexts where the opponent is right, then proposes a position that serves both sides' interests.
cards.n: Best for hostile audiences; its signature move is genuine concession before advocacy.

cards.q: Contrast Rogerian and classical (Aristotelian) argument.
cards.a: Classical argument is adversarial and linear - assert, prove, refute, and win over an undecided audience. Rogerian argument is conciliatory - understand, concede, and negotiate a shared position with a resistant audience.
cards.n: Choosing between them is itself a rhetorical decision driven by audience hostility.

cards.q: State the five parts of classical (Aristotelian) arrangement in order.
cards.a: Exordium (introduction), narratio (statement of facts/background), confirmatio (proof of your case), refutatio (refutation of opposing views), peroratio (conclusion).
cards.n: Notice that refutation comes before the conclusion: address the counterargument, then close.

cards.q: Define the exordium.
cards.a: The exordium is the opening that hooks the audience and establishes the speaker's credibility and goodwill, preparing listeners to be receptive before the case begins.

cards.q: Define the narratio.
cards.a: The narratio supplies the background: the facts, context, and history of the issue, told in a way that already frames the case favorably.

cards.q: Define the confirmatio.
cards.a: The confirmatio is the main body of proof, where the speaker develops the argument by presenting claims, evidence, and reasoning in support of the thesis.

cards.q: Define the refutatio.
cards.a: The refutatio anticipates and answers opposing arguments, conceding what is reasonable and rebutting what is not, so the audience's objections are removed before the close.

cards.q: Define the peroratio.
cards.a: The peroratio is the conclusion: it summarizes the case, amplifies its stakes, and makes the final emotional appeal or call to action.

cards.q: Contrast inductive and deductive reasoning.
cards.a: Induction moves from specific observations to a general, probable conclusion. Deduction moves from a general premise to a specific conclusion that must follow if the premises are true.
cards.n: Induction yields probability, deduction yields necessity - a distinction MC questions test directly.

cards.q: Define a syllogism and give an example.
cards.a: A syllogism is a deductive form with a major premise, a minor premise, and a conclusion. Example: All published editorials are opinion pieces (major); this column is a published editorial (minor); therefore this column is an opinion piece.
cards.n: A syllogism can be valid but unsound: valid form plus a false premise guarantees nothing about whether the conclusion is true.

cards.q: Define an enthymeme.
cards.a: An enthymeme is a syllogism with a premise left unstated because the audience is assumed to share it. Example: 'She should be trusted with the budget - she has never missed a deadline,' assuming punctual people handle money responsibly.
cards.n: Enthymemes are where warrants hide; naming the missing premise is a classic AP analysis move.

cards.q: Explain why writers use enthymemes rather than full syllogisms.
cards.a: Leaving a premise unstated is efficient and flattering: it lets the audience supply the assumption themselves, which makes them feel they reasoned to the conclusion and makes the shared value seem obvious rather than debatable.

cards.q: Define concession and refutation as argumentative moves.
cards.a: Concession grants that part of the opposing view has merit; refutation then shows why that view is nonetheless inadequate or outweighed. Used together, they build ethos and defuse objections.
cards.n: 'While it is true that... , the more pressing consideration is...' is the standard concession-refutation frame.

cards.q: Define the fallacy of ad hominem and give a one-line example.
cards.a: Attacking the person making the argument instead of the argument itself. Example: 'You cannot take her climate proposal seriously - she flies private jets.'

cards.q: Define the fallacy of straw man and give a one-line example.
cards.a: Misrepresenting an opponent's position as a weaker or more extreme version, then refuting that version. Example: 'My opponent wants to cut the arts budget, so apparently she thinks music is worthless.'

cards.q: Define the fallacy of false dilemma (either/or) and give a one-line example.
cards.a: Presenting only two options when more exist. Example: 'Either we ban phones in school or we accept that students will never learn.'

cards.q: Define the fallacy of slippery slope and give a one-line example.
cards.a: Claiming one step will inevitably trigger a chain ending in disaster, without showing the links. Example: 'If we allow late homework, soon no one will turn in anything at all.'

cards.q: Define the fallacy of hasty generalization and give a one-line example.
cards.a: Drawing a broad conclusion from a sample too small or unrepresentative to support it. Example: 'Two students cheated on the exam, so this generation has no integrity.'

cards.q: Define the fallacy of post hoc ergo propter hoc and give a one-line example.
cards.a: Assuming that because B followed A, A caused B. Example: 'Test scores rose after we repainted the school, so the paint improved learning.'

cards.q: Define the fallacy of circular reasoning (begging the question) and give a one-line example.
cards.a: Assuming in the premises the very conclusion being argued for. Example: 'This novel is the greatest of the decade because no other book from the decade is as good.'

cards.q: Define the fallacy of appeal to authority (fallacious) and give a one-line example.
cards.a: Treating a person's status as proof, when they are outside their expertise or the claim needs evidence. Example: 'A famous actor endorses this supplement, so it must be effective.'

cards.q: Define the fallacy of appeal to popularity (bandwagon) and give a one-line example.
cards.a: Arguing something is true or right because many people believe or do it. Example: 'Millions of users can't be wrong - the app must be safe.'

cards.q: Define the fallacy of appeal to fear and give a one-line example.
cards.a: Substituting an alarming consequence for evidence in order to force agreement. Example: 'Vote against this measure or your family will not be safe in this town.'

cards.q: Define the fallacy of appeal to tradition and give a one-line example.
cards.a: Arguing that something is right or best because it has always been done that way. Example: 'We have opened with the same ceremony for ninety years, so it should not change.'

cards.q: Define the fallacy of appeal to ignorance and give a one-line example.
cards.a: Claiming something is true because it has not been proven false, or false because unproven. Example: 'No study has proven the additive harmful, so it is perfectly safe.'

cards.q: Define the fallacy of red herring and give a one-line example.
cards.a: Introducing an irrelevant issue to divert attention from the actual question. Example: 'You ask about the budget shortfall, but what about how well our team played this season?'

cards.q: Define the fallacy of non sequitur and give a one-line example.
cards.a: Drawing a conclusion that does not follow logically from the premises given. Example: 'She reads a great deal, so she would make an excellent treasurer.'

cards.q: Define the fallacy of equivocation and give a one-line example.
cards.a: Shifting the meaning of a key term partway through the argument. Example: 'Only man is rational; no woman is a man; therefore no woman is rational.'

cards.q: Define the fallacy of false analogy and give a one-line example.
cards.a: Comparing two things that differ in the respect essential to the argument. Example: 'Running a country is just like running a household budget, so the nation should never borrow.'

cards.q: Define the fallacy of composition and division and give a one-line example.
cards.a: Composition assumes what is true of the parts is true of the whole; division assumes what is true of the whole is true of each part. Example: 'Every player is a star, so the team is unbeatable' (composition); 'It is a wealthy nation, so its citizens are wealthy' (division).

cards.q: Define the fallacy of loaded question and give a one-line example.
cards.a: Asking a question that presupposes an unproven claim, so any direct answer concedes it. Example: 'Why does the administration keep wasting student fees?'

cards.q: Define the fallacy of tu quoque and give a one-line example.
cards.a: Deflecting criticism by charging the critic with the same fault, as if that answered the claim. Example: 'You say I should recycle, but you drive to work every day.'

cards.q: Define the fallacy of no true Scotsman and give a one-line example.
cards.a: Rescuing a generalization from counterexamples by redefining the category to exclude them. Example: 'No serious scientist doubts this. - Dr. Vance does. - Then he is not a serious scientist.'

cards.q: Define the fallacy of cherry picking and give a one-line example.
cards.a: Citing only the data that supports the claim while suppressing contrary evidence. Example: 'Sales rose in March and June, proving the campaign worked' - omitting the four months sales fell.

cards.q: Define the fallacy of moving the goalposts and give a one-line example.
cards.a: Dismissing evidence that meets the agreed standard by demanding a new, higher one. Example: 'Fine, the trial worked, but I will not accept it until it is replicated in ten countries.'

cards.q: Explain how to write about a fallacy in an essay without simply naming it.
cards.a: Name the move, quote the specific words that make it, explain what the reasoning assumes or skips, and state the effect on the audience. Naming alone is labeling; the analysis is in the gap you expose.
cards.n: MC questions rarely ask for fallacy names; they ask what a passage's reasoning fails to establish.

cards.q: Define a line of reasoning.
cards.a: A line of reasoning is the logical sequence of claims and supporting evidence that connects the thesis to the conclusion - the order in which ideas build so that each paragraph makes the next one possible.
cards.n: Row B rewards a line of reasoning: paragraphs in an arbitrary order cost points even when each is well written.

cards.q: Explain how to test whether an essay has a line of reasoning.
cards.a: Read only the topic sentences in order. If they form a coherent argument that arrives at the thesis, the line of reasoning holds; if they read as an unordered list of observations, it does not.
cards.n: This topic-sentence test is the fastest self-check in the final minutes of an FRQ.

cards.q: Explain the function of a topic sentence.
cards.a: A topic sentence states the paragraph's subclaim and links it to the thesis, telling the reader what this paragraph will prove and why it comes here. It should assert, not announce or summarize the source.
cards.n: 'In source B, the author discusses cost' is an announcement; a topic sentence must make an arguable point.

cards.q: Define unity in a paragraph.
cards.a: Unity means every sentence in the paragraph supports the single idea named in the topic sentence; nothing wanders into a different claim.

cards.q: Define coherence in writing.
cards.a: Coherence means the sentences and paragraphs connect so the reader can follow the movement of thought, achieved through transitions, repeated key terms, pronoun reference, and consistent order.

cards.q: Explain the standard structure of an argumentative body paragraph.
cards.a: Topic sentence stating the subclaim; specific evidence introduced with context; commentary explaining how the evidence proves the subclaim; and a link sentence tying the subclaim back to the thesis or forward to the next.
cards.n: Aim for at least two sentences of commentary for every one sentence of evidence.

cards.q: Decide when to start a new paragraph.
cards.a: Start a new paragraph when the subclaim changes, when a new source or piece of evidence requires its own analysis, when shifting from your case to the counterargument, or when a paragraph has grown so long the reader loses the claim.

cards.q: Identify transitions that signal addition and state what they do to the line of reasoning.
cards.a: Addition: furthermore, moreover, in addition, also, likewise. They signal to the reader that what follows adds another item of the same kind.

cards.q: Identify transitions that signal contrast and state what they do to the line of reasoning.
cards.a: Contrast: however, yet, nevertheless, on the other hand, conversely. They signal to the reader that what follows opposes or turns against what came before.

cards.q: Identify transitions that signal causation and state what they do to the line of reasoning.
cards.a: Causation: therefore, consequently, thus, as a result, because. They signal to the reader that what follows is the cause or the effect of what came before.

cards.q: Identify transitions that signal concession and state what they do to the line of reasoning.
cards.a: Concession: admittedly, granted, of course, to be sure, while it is true that. They signal to the reader that what follows grants a point to the other side before it is answered.

cards.q: Identify transitions that signal exemplification and state what they do to the line of reasoning.
cards.a: Exemplification: for example, for instance, specifically, to illustrate, namely. They signal to the reader that what follows is a specific instance of the general claim.

cards.q: Identify transitions that signal sequence and state what they do to the line of reasoning.
cards.a: Sequence: first, next, subsequently, meanwhile, finally. They signal to the reader that what follows comes next in an order of steps, stages, or priority.

cards.q: Identify transitions that signal emphasis and state what they do to the line of reasoning.
cards.a: Emphasis: indeed, above all, in fact, most significantly, especially. They signal to the reader that what follows is the most important point so far.

cards.q: Identify transitions that signal conclusion and state what they do to the line of reasoning.
cards.a: Conclusion: in short, ultimately, on the whole, in conclusion, therefore. They signal to the reader that what follows closes the argument or sums it up.

cards.q: Explain the most common misuse of transitions.
cards.a: Using a transition whose relationship the sentences do not actually have - most often 'however' between two agreeing sentences or 'therefore' where no cause was established. The word then signals a logic the paragraph never performs.
cards.n: MC revision questions frequently test exactly this: the right answer replaces a mismatched connective.

cards.q: Explain the method of development called narration and when a writer would choose it.
cards.a: Narration: Tells a sequence of events as a story. It is best for making an abstract problem concrete and building emotional engagement.
cards.h: → what it does + when to use

cards.q: Explain the method of development called description and when a writer would choose it.
cards.a: Description: Renders sensory and concrete detail about a subject. It is best for making a scene or condition vivid so the audience can judge it firsthand.
cards.h: → what it does + when to use

cards.q: Explain the method of development called definition and when a writer would choose it.
cards.a: Definition: Establishes what a key term means and does not mean. It is best when the argument turns on a contested term such as 'freedom' or 'fairness'.
cards.h: → what it does + when to use

cards.q: Explain the method of development called exemplification and when a writer would choose it.
cards.a: Exemplification: Supports a generalization with a series of specific instances. It is best for showing that a pattern is real and widespread rather than isolated.
